principles.name: We put members first
principles.description: When making decisions large and small, do what is right for members to make them more productive and successful, in service of creating economic opportunity.
evidence_signals: Chose member trust or quality over a short-term growth metric and explains the trade-off
Pushed back on a feature or experiment that could harm users
Connects the work to members' careers or economic opportunity

principles.name: We trust and care about each other
principles.description: Start from a position of trust and practice respect, compassion, honesty and integrity with colleagues.
evidence_signals: Repaired or improved a difficult working relationship
Supported a colleague through a hard situation or helped them grow
Assumes good intent and builds trust across teams

principles.name: We are open, honest and constructive
principles.description: Seek the truth, welcome feedback, and turn hard problems into solutions through learning and candid communication.
evidence_signals: Gave or received direct feedback with care and shows what changed
Disagreed with a manager or lead openly and constructively
Explains decisions clearly and at the right altitude for the audience

principles.name: We act as One LinkedIn
principles.description: Act as owners under one vision, put the whole company ahead of the local team, and recognize collective impact.
evidence_signals: Drove an initiative across team boundaries without being asked
Made a trade-off that helped the company even when it cost their own team
Uses 'I' for own decisions and credits partners for shared outcomes

principles.name: We embody diversity, inclusion and belonging
principles.description: Welcome different perspectives, ensure fair access to opportunity, and help build a fair, accessible world of work.
evidence_signals: Actively sought out or amplified a different perspective that changed a decision
Made a process, product or team more accessible or fair
Mentored or sponsored people from under-represented backgrounds

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Background and logistics. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Technical phone screen
rounds.notes: One or two coding problems. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Onsite coding (two rounds)
rounds.notes: Data structures and algorithms. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: System design
rounds.notes: Usually a LinkedIn-like product: feed, notifications, People You May Know, search, messaging, top-K.

rounds.name: Technical communication
rounds.notes: Candidate explains a past project in depth; the interviewer probes design decisions and clarity of explanation.

rounds.name: Host manager
rounds.notes: Walks through each prior role: why the candidate left, team size, own contribution; behavioral and values questions.

rounds.name: HR phone screen
rounds.notes: Background and motivation. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: PM phone screen
rounds.notes: Product design and analytics questions; one or two calls.

rounds.name: Product design
rounds.notes: About half of reported PM questions; improve or design a LinkedIn feature.

rounds.name: Analytics / metrics
rounds.interviewer_role: Senior product manager or data scientist
rounds.notes: Success metrics, A/B tests and diagnosing metric drops.

rounds.name: Behavioral and leadership
rounds.notes: Why LinkedIn, PM principles, collaboration and values.

rounds.name: Strategy
rounds.notes: Business strategy and vision for the product area; no coding for PMs.

question_patterns.pattern: A time the candidate chose user trust or long-term value over a short-term metric, or opposed a feature that could harm users
A time the candidate gave hard feedback or disagreed with a manager or lead, and how it was received
values: We are open, honest and constructive

question_patterns.pattern: A cancelled or failed project and what the candidate did immediately afterward
values: We are open, honest and constructive

question_patterns.pattern: How the candidate improved a difficult working relationship across teams
values: We trust and care about each other

question_patterns.pattern: A time the candidate created opportunity for others or brought in a perspective that was missing
values: We embody diversity, inclusion and belonging

question_patterns.pattern: Each previous role: what the team did, its size, the candidate's contribution, and why they moved on
An initiative the candidate drove across team boundaries without being asked
Explain a past project to an engineer from another team, defending each major design decision
values: We are open, honest and constructive

question_patterns.pattern: Design a LinkedIn-style product such as the feed, notifications, connection suggestions or search at very large scale
Design a system that counts or ranks events over a sliding time window, such as top-K or profile views
Pick a member segment and improve a LinkedIn feature such as profile, messaging, onboarding or endorsements
Define success for a feature, design an A/B test, or diagnose a drop in a key metric
Reason about a strategic business decision such as an acquisition, a new market or a subscription product

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you chose user trust or product quality over a growth metric.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describes the metric at stake and the risk to users (spam, privacy, misleading UX), the data gathered, and how the candidate argued the case to stakeholders. States the decision, the measured effect on trust and long-term engagement, and any metric given up. Signals: member-first judgment backed by evidence, not just principle. Pitfall: a story with no real trade-off.

looking_for: Whether you put users ahead of short-term metrics
How you back your judgment with evidence
strong_signals: Names the metric at stake and the risk to users
Explains how you argued the case to stakeholders
Shows the measured effect, including what was given up
watch_outs: A story with no real trade-off
Principles with no data behind them

sample_questions.question: Describe a time you had to give constructive feedback under pressure.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Sets the context and why the feedback could not wait. Explains how the candidate prepared, delivered it privately and specifically, and listened. Shows the outcome for the person and the work, and how the relationship held. Signals: candor with care, structured communication. Pitfall: harsh feedback framed as honesty, or avoiding the conversation.
values: We are open, honest and constructive
We trust and care about each other

looking_for: Whether you give candid feedback with care
How you prepare for a hard conversation
strong_signals: Explains why the feedback could not wait
Delivers it privately and specifically, then listens
Shows the relationship held

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a project that was cancelled or failed. What did you do right after?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Owns the candidate's part in the failure, explains the cause honestly, and focuses on the quick next step: what was salvaged, how the team re-focused, what changed in the candidate's approach. Shows resilience and moving to the next play without dwelling. Pitfall: blaming leadership or presenting it as nobody's fault.
values: We are open, honest and constructive

looking_for: Your resilience after a setback
Whether you own your part honestly
strong_signals: Explains the cause honestly
Shows what was salvaged and how the team refocused
Names what changed in your approach

sample_questions.question: Describe how you improved a difficult working relationship.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Explains the friction and its impact on work, the candidate's own contribution to the problem, and concrete steps: a direct conversation, understanding the other person's goals, agreeing on working norms. Shows a lasting improvement and a shared result. Pitfall: the other person changed and the candidate did nothing.
values: We trust and care about each other

looking_for: How you repair friction at work
Whether you see your own part in the problem
strong_signals: Names your own contribution to the friction
Describes a direct conversation and agreed working norms
Shows a lasting improvement
watch_outs: The other person changed and you did nothing
No impact on the work described

sample_questions.question: Tell me about an intelligent risk you took and how you sized it.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describes the opportunity and the downside, how the candidate estimated likelihood and impact, and how they limited exposure (experiment, flag, phased rollout). Gives the outcome and what they would size differently. Signals: calculated, not reckless, with excellence in execution. Pitfall: a risk with no analysis.

looking_for: How you weigh likelihood and impact
Whether you limit exposure before acting
strong_signals: Explains how you estimated the downside
Uses flags, experiments or phased rollouts
Says what you would size differently

sample_questions.question: How has your work created economic opportunity for other people?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Connects a concrete project or action to people's jobs, skills or income: a hiring tool, mentoring, a product that helped small businesses, open source used by others. Quantifies reach where possible and reflects on why it matters to the candidate. Ties to LinkedIn's mission without sounding scripted. Pitfall: vague claims with no people affected.
values: We embody diversity, inclusion and belonging

looking_for: Whether your work has helped people grow
How genuinely you connect to the mission
strong_signals: Links a concrete project to people's jobs, skills or income
Quantifies reach where possible
Explains why it matters to you
watch_outs: Vague claims with no people affected

sample_questions.question: Walk me through each of your previous jobs: what the team did, how big it was, what you contributed and why you left.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Keeps each role brief and structured: team mission and size, the candidate's own scope and one notable result, and a positive reason for moving on. Shows a clear growth arc toward this role. Is ready for deep follow-ups on any role. Pitfall: long rambling history or negative comments about past employers.

looking_for: Your growth arc toward this role
Whether you can summarize each role clearly
strong_signals: Keeps each role brief: team, scope and one result
Gives a positive reason for each move
Handles deep follow-ups on any role

sample_questions.question: Tell me about an initiative you drove that nobody asked you to do.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Explains the gap, why it mattered to the business or members, how the candidate built support across teams and delivered, and the measurable result. Shows judgment in choosing this over assigned work and that the work outlived the candidate's involvement. Pitfall: going rogue without alignment.

looking_for: Whether you spot gaps and act on them
Your judgment in choosing this over assigned work
strong_signals: Explains why the gap mattered
Builds support across teams before delivering
Shows the work lasted beyond your involvement

sample_questions.question: Why LinkedIn, and why this role?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Connects personal motivation to the mission of economic opportunity, shows knowledge of the product area and its members, and explains what the candidate would bring and want to learn. Specific and honest. Pitfall: generic praise or answers about compensation and brand only.

looking_for: Whether your motivation connects to the mission
How well you know the product area and its users
strong_signals: Is specific about the product area
Says what you bring and want to learn
watch_outs: Talking only about compensation or brand

sample_questions.question: Explain a project you worked on in depth to an engineer from another team, including the decisions you made.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Starts with the problem and why it mattered, then a high-level architecture before details. Covers two or three key decisions with alternatives and trade-offs, how the candidate validated them, and what they would change. Adjusts depth to the listener and answers follow-ups precisely. Pitfall: jargon-heavy detail without structure, or not knowing why decisions were made.
values: We are open, honest and constructive

looking_for: How clearly you explain technical work to another engineer
Whether you know why decisions were made
strong_signals: Starts with the problem, then the high-level architecture
Covers key decisions with alternatives
Adjusts depth to the listener
watch_outs: Unable to explain why a choice was made

sample_questions.question: Design the LinkedIn feed for members with very different network sizes.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarifies requirements and scale, then covers fan-out on write versus read with a hybrid for high-follower accounts, candidate generation and ranking, caching, and freshness. Discusses member-first concerns like low-quality content and notification fatigue. Explains bottlenecks and failure handling, and ties choices to member and business impact. Pitfall: ignoring the celebrity fan-out problem.

looking_for: How you handle users with very different network sizes
Whether you tie design choices to user impact
strong_signals: Uses a hybrid of fan-out on write and on read
Separates candidate generation from ranking
Considers low-quality content and notification fatigue

sample_questions.question: Design a service that tracks events over a sliding time window and returns the top K, for example most viewed items in the last hour.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarifies accuracy versus latency needs. Covers streaming ingestion, windowed counting (bucketed counters, count-min sketch for approximation), merging partial top-K across partitions, and storage of results. Discusses exactness trade-offs, late events, and scaling. Pitfall: recomputing everything from raw logs on each request.

looking_for: How you count events over time windows at scale
Whether you weigh exactness against latency
strong_signals: Uses bucketed or approximate counters
Merges partial top-K results across partitions
Handles late events
watch_outs: Recomputing from raw logs on every request

sample_questions.question: How would you design a 'People You May Know' recommendation system for a very large professional network?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Separates candidate generation (second-degree connections, shared schools or companies) from ranking with features and a model. Discusses offline precompute versus online serving, graph storage and partitioning, cold start for new members, and privacy limits. Defines how success is measured. Pitfall: a full graph traversal per request.

looking_for: How you design recommendations on a huge graph
Whether you separate candidate generation from ranking
strong_signals: Discusses offline precompute versus online serving
Handles cold start for new members
Respects privacy limits and defines success
watch_outs: A full graph traversal per request

sample_questions.question: How would you improve LinkedIn's skill endorsements feature?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarifies the goal of endorsements (trust signal for recruiters, engagement) and the users on both sides. Identifies problems such as low signal quality, then proposes and prioritizes improvements (context, verification, prompts). Defines success metrics and guardrails like spam. Pitfall: adding engagement prompts that make the signal worse.

looking_for: Whether you clarify the feature's goal
How you serve both sides of the feature
strong_signals: Names problems like low signal quality
Prioritizes improvements clearly
Defines success metrics and spam guardrails
watch_outs: Engagement prompts that weaken the signal

sample_questions.question: How would you redesign the LinkedIn profile page?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Picks a segment (job seekers, recruiters viewing profiles, students) and the job the profile does for them. Finds key pains, proposes a few changes, and prioritizes by impact on member outcomes. Considers both the profile owner and the viewer. Defines metrics such as profile completeness and recruiter contact rate. Pitfall: visual redesign with no user goal.

looking_for: Whether you start from a user goal
How you balance the profile owner and the viewer
strong_signals: Picks a segment and the job the profile does for them
Prioritizes changes by member outcomes
Defines metrics such as recruiter contact rate
watch_outs: A visual redesign with no user goal

sample_questions.question: How would you measure the success of the skills and endorsements feature?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Starts from the feature's goal, then lists metrics by funnel: adoption, engagement, and value delivered (recruiter searches using skills, member outcomes). Picks one primary metric with guardrails and explains how to validate it with an experiment. Pitfall: listing every metric with no priority.

looking_for: How you tie metrics to a feature's goal
Whether you can choose one primary metric
strong_signals: Organizes metrics by funnel stage
Picks one primary metric with guardrails
Explains how to validate with an experiment
watch_outs: Listing every metric with no priority
Metrics with no link to the goal

sample_questions.question: After a change to the sign-up flow, retention dropped by 2 percent. How would you respond?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Checks data validity first, then segments by platform, region, cohort and acquisition channel, and compares with the change timeline. Forms hypotheses linked to the sign-up change, proposes analyses or a rollback test, and decides based on the trade-off with whatever the change improved. Pitfall: jumping to a single cause without checking the data.

looking_for: How you structure an investigation of a metric drop
Whether you check the data before looking for causes
strong_signals: Segments by platform, cohort and channel
Links hypotheses to the sign-up change
Weighs the drop against what the change improved

sample_questions.question: How would you design an A/B test for the People You May Know feature?
sample_questions.strong_answer: States the hypothesis and primary metric (accepted invites, meaningful connections), guardrails (spam reports, invite declines), and the unit of randomization. Addresses network effects between test and control and how to handle them (cluster randomization). Covers sample size and duration. Pitfall: ignoring interference in a social graph.

looking_for: How you design a sound experiment
Whether you account for network effects
strong_signals: States the hypothesis, primary metric and guardrails
Picks the right unit of randomization
Covers sample size and duration
watch_outs: Ignoring interference between test and control

sample_questions.question: How would you improve retention for LinkedIn Premium subscribers?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Segments subscribers by reason for buying (job seekers, sales, recruiters) and diagnoses why each churns, for example after landing a job. Proposes targeted levers and prioritizes them, considering revenue and member value. Defines retention metrics and an experiment plan. Pitfall: one discount for everyone.

looking_for: How you segment subscribers by need
Whether you diagnose churn before proposing fixes
strong_signals: Explains why each segment churns
Prioritizes targeted levers
Defines retention metrics and an experiment plan

bar_by_level.scope_expectation: Builds features inside a defined area; larger design decisions are made by someone more senior.
Owns a system or service end to end; a career level where engineers may stay long term.
Sets technical direction for an area that several teams depend on.
Owns technical strategy across an organization and resolves disagreements between staff engineers.
Sets direction for a major part of LinkedIn's technology.
Owns a product area's strategy, metrics and roadmap and leads cross-functional partners.

persona.pace: Steady and structured, with time for deep follow-ups
persona.pushback_style: Asks the candidate to explain decisions more clearly, at the right level, and how members were affected
persona.closing_style: Leaves time for the candidate's questions about the team and mission

case_style.notes: Product design dominates PM cases (about half of reported questions), followed by analytics and A/B testing; strategy questions are less common.

sources.title: What to expect in the LinkedIn system design interview

low_confidence_notes: values_framework: LinkedIn's older six values (members first, relationships matter, act like an owner, take intelligent risks, and others) still appear in prep guides; we use the five shared values on the current careers page. Weights are our estimate.

loop_structure: the Glassdoor review was seen only in search results (the page blocks fetching); the technical communication and host manager rounds are reported in several sources but may vary by team.
loop_structure: PM round names and durations are inferred from a prep guide that lists question shares, not an official LinkedIn page.
bar_by_level: IC mapping comes from a third-party guide; one other guide uses E4 to E6 labels instead. PM level names are generic.
scoring_weights: no public source gives weights; communication is weighted up because several guides say the loop grades clarity of explanation explicitly.
